Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157309 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-dddb9707-e886-593b-b435-6f7cb6f00a64" "question-15726506-9b26-5fcb-965d-d1bfeaeef6e9" "question-7876349f-b735-5751-9a1b-0e3749e49e68" "question-840811f2-e29f-518b-8c90-d58cbee9a3ee" "question-5019f447-273c-518d-a2e4-ccc53ac4a221"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157113 :question/worked-solution "A Poisson random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{\lambda^x e^{-\lambda}}{x!}
$$

Let $X$ be the number of prank calls received by the telephone exchange. Since the average rate is $3$ prank calls per day, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, the number of prank calls can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate $\lambda = 3,$ and we can write $X\sim \textrm{Po}(3).$

So, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{3^x e^{-3}}{x!}
$$

Therefore, the probability of receiving $5$ prank calls is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=5) & =f(5) \\  & =\frac{{3}^{5}{e}^{-3}}{5!} \\  & ≈0.101\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157310 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-f7f3a56e-4b53-5169-b909-9f25434c0fc1" "question-1343b72e-5bbd-541b-8ed3-38578a085bf3" "question-ff042347-0e79-58c2-92e7-81e42f1921f1" "question-f608fe3c-6d97-51bc-b0a2-012a45774f2c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157114 :question/worked-solution "A Poisson random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{\lambda^x e^{-\lambda}}{x!}
$$

Let $X$ be the number of traffic accidents. Since the average rate is $4$ traffic accidents per week, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, the number of traffic accidents can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate $\lambda = 4,$ and we can write $X\sim \textrm{Po}(4).$

So, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{4^x e^{-4}}{x!}
$$

Therefore, the probability of finding fewer than $3$ traffic accidents on the next week is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<3) & =P(X\in {0,1,2}) \\  & =f(0)+f(1)+f(2) \\  & =\frac{{4}^{0}{e}^{-4}}{0!}+\frac{{4}^{1}{e}^{-4}}{1!}+\frac{{4}^{2}{e}^{-4}}{2!} \\  & ={e}^{-4}(\frac{{4}^{0}}{0!}+\frac{{4}^{1}}{1!}+\frac{{4}^{2}}{2!}) \\  & ≈0.238\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157311 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-61a1ddbb-f5ab-5fff-b498-6bc2ff368bd2" "question-2a680a24-a0a8-52d9-a8a7-fff48b164489" "question-d55083ad-b1c4-5352-954c-42f5ad322bca"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157115 :question/worked-solution "A Poisson random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{\lambda^x e^{-\lambda}}{x!}
$$

Let $X$ be the number of machines with a fault in the factory. Since the average rate is $3$ faulty machines per week, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, the number of machines with faults can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate $\lambda = 3,$ and we can write $X\sim \textrm{Po}(3).$

So, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{3^x e^{-3}}{x!}
$$

To compute $P(X \geq 2),$ we will use the complement:

$$
P(X \geq 2) = 1 - P(X<  2)
$$

Computing the probability of the complement, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<2) & =P(X\in {0,1}) \\  & =f(0)+f(1) \\  & =\frac{{3}^{0}{e}^{-3}}{0!}+\frac{{3}^{1}{e}^{-3}}{1!} \\  & ≈0.199\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Therefore, the probability of at least $2$ machines registering a fault next week is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 2) & =1-P(X<2) \\  & ≈1-0.199 \\  & ≈0.801\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-2a75eec7-e20c-53a7-afe2-6cf4faf6becf" :question/id #uuid "2a75eec7-e20c-53a7-afe2-6cf4faf6becf" :question/math-academy-id "q-131311" :question/problem "Which of the following random variables could be modeled using a Poisson distribution?

:question/problem "At a dental clinic, patients arrive at an average rate of $10$ patients every hour during the hours when the clinic is open. What is the probability that exactly $5$ customers will arrive in the next hour? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places. You may assume that patients arrive independently and at a constant average rate." :question/worked-solution "A Poisson random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{\lambda }^{x}{e}^{-\lambda }}{x!}
$$

Let $X$ be the number of patients who will arrive in the next hour. Since the average rate is $10$ patients every hour when the clinic is open, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, the number of patients can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate $\lambda =10,$ and we can write $X∼\text{Po}(10).$

So, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{10}^{x}{e}^{-10}}{x!}
$$

If the rate of the events is $\lambda,$ then the number of events $x$ occurring in an interval of fixed length has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{\lambda^x e^{-\lambda}}{x!}, \qquad x=0,1,2,3, \ldots
$$

If a random variable $X$ follows a Poisson distribution with rate $\lambda,$ then we write $X \sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda).$

For example, suppose that calls come in at an average rate of $3$ calls per minute at a call center. Then the number of calls $X$ that are received during the next minute has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{3^x e^{-3}}{x!}
$$

In particular, the probability of receiving $4$ calls during the next minute is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=4) & =f(4) \\  & =\frac{{3}^{4}{e}^{-3}}{4!} \\  & ≈0.168\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186158493 :tutorial/content "The shape of the graph of the Poisson distribution depends on the value of $\lambda.$ When $\lambda$ is small, the probability is concentrated at small values of $x.$ When $\lambda$ is larger, the probability is concentrated at larger values of $x.$

rounded to $3$ decimal places." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157311 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-61a1ddbb-f5ab-5fff-b498-6bc2ff368bd2" "question-2a680a24-a0a8-52d9-a8a7-fff48b164489" "question-d55083ad-b1c4-5352-954c-42f5ad322bca"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157115 :question/worked-solution "A Poisson random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{\lambda^x e^{-\lambda}}{x!}

Let $X$ be the number of machines with a fault in the factory. Since the average rate is $3$ faulty machines per week, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, the number of machines with faults can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate $\lambda = 3,$ and we can write $X\sim \textrm{Po}(3).$

So, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{3^x e^{-3}}{x!}
$$

To compute $P(X \geq 2),$ we will use the complement:

$$
P(X \geq 2) = 1 - P(X<  2)
$$

Computing the probability of the complement, we get

$$

$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 2) & =1-P(X<2) \\  & ≈1-0.199 \\  & ≈0.801\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-2a75eec7-e20c-53a7-afe2-6cf4faf6becf" :question/id #uuid "2a75eec7-e20c-53a7-afe2-6cf4faf6becf" :question/math-academy-id "q-131311" :question/problem "Which of the following random variables could be modeled using a Poisson distribution?

- The number of calls a firm will receive next week for help concerning a toy" :question/worked-solution "A Poisson distribution models the number of events that occur in an interval of time or space if events occur independently and at a constant average rate.

With that in mind, let's consider each of the given random variables.

- Random variable I does *not* follow a Poisson distribution. The average points scored on the math test is not an event that occurs at a constant average rate.

- Random variable II follows a Poisson distribution. The number of orders can be modeled as independent events with a constant average rate, and we wish to know how many events occur in an interval of time (a month).

- Random variable III follows a Poisson distribution. Again, the number of calls can be modeled as independent events with a constant average rate, and we wish to know how many events occur in an interval of time (a week).

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0bc8a185-a6bc-582b-bc0a-ce5101e00aad"] :db/ensure You may assume that patients arrive independently and at a constant average rate." :question/worked-solution "A Poisson random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{\lambda }^{x}{e}^{-\lambda }}{x!}
$$

Let $X$ be the number of patients who will arrive in the next hour. Since the average rate is $10$ patients every hour when the clinic is open, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, the number of patients can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate $\lambda =10,$ and we can write $X∼\text{Po}(10).$

So, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{10}^{x}{e}^{-10}}{x!}
$$

Therefore, the probability that exactly $5$ customers will arrive in the next hour while the clinic is open is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=5) & =f(5) \\  & =\frac{{10}^{5}{e}^{-10}}{5!} \\  & ≈0.038\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a25a9175-9800-575a-9d19-a0e2a647d011"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Since the average rate is $9$ wedding dresses sold per week, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, the number of wedding dresses sold can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate $\lambda =9,$ and we can write $X∼\text{Po}(9).$ 

So, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{9}^{x}{e}^{-9}}{x!}
$$

To compute $P(X>3),$ we will use the complement:

$$
P(X>3)=1-P(X\le 3)
$$

Computing the probability of the complement, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 3) & =P(X\in {0,1,2,3}) \\  & =f(0)+f(1)+f(2)+f(3) \\  & =\frac{{9}^{0}{e}^{-9}}{0!}+\frac{{9}^{1}{e}^{-9}}{1!}+\frac{{9}^{2}{e}^{-9}}{2!}+\frac{{9}^{3}{e}^{-9}}{3!} \\  & ≈0.021\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Therefore, the probability of selling more than $3$ wedding dresses next week is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>3) & =1-P(X\le 3) \\  & ≈1-0.021 \\  & =0.979\end{aligned}
$$

If the rate of the events is $\lambda,$ then the number of events $x$ occurring in an interval of fixed length has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{\lambda^x e^{-\lambda}}{x!}, \qquad x=0,1,2,3, \ldots
$$

If a random variable $X$ follows a Poisson distribution with rate $\lambda,$ then we write $X \sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda).$

For example, suppose that calls come in at an average rate of $3$ calls per minute at a call center. Then the number of calls $X$ that are received during the next minute has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{3^x e^{-3}}{x!}
$$

In particular, the probability of receiving $4$ calls during the next minute is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=4) & =f(4) \\  & =\frac{{3}^{4}{e}^{-3}}{4!} \\  & ≈0.168\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186158493 :tutorial/content "The shape of the graph of the Poisson distribution depends on the value of $\lambda.$ When $\lambda$ is small, the probability is concentrated at small values of $x.$ When $\lambda$ is larger, the probability is concentrated at larger values of $x.$

$$
f(x)=\frac{{10}^{x}{e}^{-10}}{x!}
$$

$$

$$

["question-15726506-9b26-5fcb-965d-d1bfeaeef6e9" :question/math-academy-id "q-131266"] ["question-15726506-9b26-5fcb-965d-d1bfeaeef6e9" :question/problem "Large metal sheets have faults in random positions but, on average, there is one fault per $10\,{\text{m}}^{2}.$ What is the probability that the next sheet of size $5\,\text{m}\times 8\,\text{m}$ will have exactly one fault? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places. You may assume that faults occur independently and at a constant average rate."] ["question-15726506-9b26-5fcb-965d-d1bfeaeef6e9" :question/worked-solution "A Poisson random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{\lambda }^{x}{e}^{-\lambda }}{x!}
$$

Let $X$ be the number of faults in the next sheet of area $40\,{\text{m}}^{2}\,(5\,\text{m}\times 8\,\text{m}).$ Since there is on average $1$ fault per  $10\,{\text{m}}^{2}$, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, we expect $4$ faults in a sheet of size $40\,{\text{m}}^{2}.$ So, the number of faults in a $5\,\text{m}\times 8\,\text{m}$ metal sheet can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate $\lambda =4,$ and we can write $X∼\text{Po}(4).$

So, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{4}^{x}{e}^{-4}}{x!}
$$

Therefore, the probability that the next $5\,\text{m}\times 8\,\text{m}$ metal sheet will have exactly $1$ fault is

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 3) & =P(X\in {0,1,2,3}) \\  & =f(0)+f(1)+f(2)+f(3) \\  & =\frac{{5}^{0}{e}^{-5}}{0!}+\frac{{5}^{1}{e}^{-5}}{1!}+\frac{{5}^{2}{e}^{-5}}{2!}+\frac{{5}^{3}{e}^{-5}}{3!} \\  & ≈0.265\end{aligned}

["question-61a1ddbb-f5ab-5fff-b498-6bc2ff368bd2" :question/math-academy-id "q-85390"] ["question-61a1ddbb-f5ab-5fff-b498-6bc2ff368bd2" :question/problem "On average, every batch of televisions has $5$ defective televisions in a television factory. What is the probability that the factory will produce more than $2$ defective televisions in the next batch? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places. You may assume that defective televisions occur independently and at a constant average rate."] ["question-61a1ddbb-f5ab-5fff-b498-6bc2ff368bd2" :question/worked-solution "A Poisson random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{\lambda }^{x}{e}^{-\lambda }}{x!}
$$

Let $X$ be the number of televisions produced with defects. Since the average rate is $5$ televisions with defects per batch, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, the number of televisions with defects can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate $\lambda =5,$ and we can write $X∼\text{Po}(5).$ 

So, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{5}^{x}{e}^{-5}}{x!}
$$

To compute $P(X>2),$ we will use the complement:

$$
P(X>2)=1-P(X\le 2)
$$

Computing the probability of the complement, we get

$$

"question-d55083ad-b1c4-5352-954c-42f5ad322bca"] [17592186158491 :tutorial/content "A **Poisson distribution** is a probability distribution that models the number of events that occur in an interval of time or space if events occur independently and at a constant average rate.

If the rate of the events is $\lambda,$ then the number of events $x$ occurring in an interval of fixed length has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{\lambda^x e^{-\lambda}}{x!}, \qquad x=0,1,2,3, \ldots
$$

If a random variable $X$ follows a Poisson distribution with rate $\lambda,$ then we write $X \sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda).$

For example, suppose that calls come in at an average rate of $3$ calls per minute at a call center. Then the number of calls $X$ that are received during the next minute has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{3^x e^{-3}}{x!}
$$

In particular, the probability of receiving $4$ calls during the next minute is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=4) & =f(4) \\  & =\frac{{3}^{4}{e}^{-3}}{4!} \\  & ≈0.168\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places."] [17592186158493 :tutorial/content "The shape of the graph of the Poisson distribution depends on the value of $\lambda.$ When $\lambda$ is small, the probability is concentrated at small values of $x.$ When $\lambda$ is larger, the probability is concentrated at larger values of $x.$

27841} {:db/id 17592186158167 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158491 :tutorial/content "A **Poisson distribution** is a probability distribution that models the number of events that occur in an interval of time or space if events occur independently and at a constant average rate.

If the rate of the events is $\lambda$, then the number of events $x$ occurring in an interval of fixed length has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{\lambda^x e^{-\lambda}}{x!}, \qquad x=0,1,2,3, \ldots
$$

If a random variable $X$ follows a Poisson distribution with rate $\lambda$, then we write $X \sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda)$.

For example, suppose that calls come in at an average rate of $3$ calls per minute at a call center. Then the number of calls $X$ that are received during the next minute has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{3^x e^{-3}}{x!}
$$

In particular, the probability of receiving $4$ calls during the next minute is

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X = 4) &= f(4) \\
&= \frac{3^{4}e^{-3}}{4!} \\
&\approx 0.168
\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places." :tutorial/id #uuid "6e07ef85-f3ca-52c8-89e2-062d8ea7c9eb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4525 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "fd4dd871-25f7-54f5-9345-a556f2356cb0" :step/math-academy-id 27850 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158170}} {:db/id 17592186158170 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158493 :tutorial/content "The shape of the graph of the Poisson distribution depends on the value of $\lambda$. If the rate of the events is $\lambda$, then the number of events $x$ occurring in an interval of fixed length has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{\lambda^x e^{-\lambda}}{x!}, \qquad x=0,1,2,3, \ldots
$$

If a random variable $X$ follows a Poisson distribution with rate $\lambda$, then we write $X \sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda)$.

For example, suppose that calls come in at an average rate of $3$ calls per minute at a call center. Then the number of calls $X$ that are received during the next minute has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{3^x e^{-3}}{x!}
$$

In particular, the probability of receiving $4$ calls during the next minute is

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X = 4) &= f(4) \\
&= \frac{3^{4}e^{-3}}{4!} \\
&\approx 0.168
\end{aligned}
$$
